Inside a conceptric

What does one claim depend on?

In The Cost of Complexity, a square stands for a memory. Dividing each square into four lets the memory distinguish more possibilities. One claim in the manuscript’s section on refinement depends entirely on how those divisions are priced.

The Cost of Complexity · Figure 3

When each division is priced by area, every round of subdivision costs the same.

Open the claim and its figure, p. 10 ↗

A conceptric is a relational container. This one holds the claim. Its exterior says which section contains it, which assumption it requires and which figure gives its grounds. Each link opens another container. An agent can follow a claim to its premise, then use the same operation to open the premise’s source.

Each container is also a state machine. Its tools are verbs, with permissions. A reader can inspect the source. An editor can propose a correction against a particular revision. When the source changes, a dependent review can go stale even while the manuscript sentence stays exactly as it was.

One claim, several relationships

The claim about equal cost per round belongs to a section, requires an assumption about how a division is priced, and is illustrated by Figure 3. Opening the section, then the claim, then its grounds uses the same operation at successively finer scales.

Changing a recorded input leaves a trail to the work that consumed it. Looking up the pricing rule brings back the relevant passage and figure. The researcher decides how the manuscript should change.

Recursive memory · Query diffusion

How does a question find its evidence?

Zoom out from Figure 3. A claim belongs to a section, the section to a paper. Each group has an exterior of its own and can be opened with the same tools. That repeated structure makes a network of conceptrics a recursive graph.

The relations do two jobs. A link such as requires tells the agent how to inspect an argument. Weighted connections between related sources help it search. In query diffusion, a question gives some records more weight, then some of that weight spreads to their neighbours. Groups bring the relevant passages into reach. Permission determines what the agent may open.

From a question to a source

Ask where the paper gets its distribution of symbol frequencies. The question leads through the paper to its discussion of rank and cost. Equation 46 gives the distribution under the stated constraint. The stored section can serve the next question, and the answer points back to the exact edition.

The Cost of Complexity · The geometry of refinement

What does another distinction cost?

Start with a square. Divide it into four quarters, then divide each quarter into four again. You can now tell sixteen places apart. The paper asks what it costs to build the apparatus that lets you make those choices.

Choose a quarter, then a cell

Each quarter is a register, a physical system that holds a set of alternatives. Picking the quarter is itself a choice. The apparatus that makes it is a register too, so it belongs in the budget.

Cost to reach a cell = cost to provide and choose its quarter + cost to choose inside it

See the register example in the paper
Choose a quarter
→
Inside quarter 2

Quarter 2, cell 3 identifies one of the sixteen places.

What does the next round cost?

In this model, each round splits every existing cell into four. Change the price of a split and advance a round. The cuts stay in the same places.

Price one split by

Each smaller square has a quarter of its parent’s area, so one split costs a quarter as much.

→

Round 2 of 4

4 splits × 1/4 unit per split = 1 unit added

Added this round
1
Total after this round
2

For each rule the first round costs 1 unit. The figures count subdivision costs.

Gold marks the cuts made in this round. The blue Hilbert path visits the cells in order and finishes each quarter before moving to the next.

What adds up

Area pricing adds one unit every time the number of cells quadruples. The total grows as log N, where N is the number of cells.

Wall-length pricing adds twice as much at each round. The total grows as √N. Pricing by width cubed halves each new contribution and the total approaches two units.

Open Figure 3 (through 64 cells) Trace a numerical check of Figure 3

When does the logarithm survive?

When the same multiplication of capacity costs the same at every size, the logarithm is exact. The paper calls that assumption homogeneous refinement.

The general bound needs a different assumption. If registers can be reused like digits and their complete costs add, a fixed-size digit repeated enough times sets a logarithmic upper bound on the cheapest design. A positive limiting price per unit of information gives logarithmic growth.

Read the positional composition theorem

Erasing a failed guess releases heat

In a model that guesses, checks and resets after failure, the erased guesses form their own distribution. With a thermal bath at temperature T initially uncorrelated with the register, and a complete reset that uses no retained side information, Landauer’s principle puts a floor on the mean heat released. The paper bounds that floor using the guesses’ probability ranks.

⟨Q⟩ ≥ kBT H ≥ kBT ⟨log r⟩

Here H is the entropy of the guesses actually erased, and r puts the most likely erased guess first.

See the guessing machine

A logarithmic price gives a family of power laws

Take a finite vocabulary where the symbol in rank r costs log r to reach. Among distributions with the same mean cost, the one with greatest entropy is a power law.

p(r) ∝ r−λ

The mean cost sets λ. The case λ = 1 is Zipf’s law on a finite vocabulary. An infinite vocabulary needs λ > 1 to normalise.

Read the rank-distribution result
Further results and evidence

The symbol-cost theorem concerns the cost of reaching a particular rank. A design needs to distinguish its entire more-typical prefix and pay for the selector and for identifying where each code ends. Under the paper’s conditions the asymptotic price per unit of information approaches the register rate.

The geometry can also change while the order stays fixed. Figure 4 puts the same hierarchy on self-similar sets of different dimensions. With wall-length pricing, the exponent decreases as the supporting set thins. In the disconnected cases the path just indicates rank order.

The paper also asks how much information a representation keeps about a chosen target. Its objective balances that fidelity against the cost of the register describing it.

Follow-up draft · 19 November 2026

What if the layout itself has to be stored?

Sixteen places can be arranged as one register of sixteen, a two-way choice followed by an eight-way choice, or other ordered ways of multiplying register sizes. Physical origins of the Kalmár constant asks how many such layouts a budget can support when the system must represent its choice of layout too. Eigen produced the draft in one pass at the author’s prompt.

What the constant measures

With no fixed cost for a register to exist, the number of layouts grows exponentially with the budget. In the draft’s units, the growth exponent is Kalmár’s constant, about 1.729.
